passage:
"Saurabh Chacha, why did the lights go off in the whole village?"
"Power cut, Yogesh. Come up to the roof. Bring the mat."
"It's so dark. I can't see anything."
"Wait. Lie down. Look up."
"...Chacha."
"Hmm?"
"There are SO many. Were they always there?"
"Always. The city lights hide them."
"That white smudge, is that a cloud?"
"That's our galaxy. Millions of stars."
"Millions? Then... we're really, really small."
"Very small."
"It's weird. I feel tiny, but I feel happy. Is that allowed?"
"It's allowed."
"I was so angry about losing the match today. It doesn't feel big anymore."
"Things look different from up here, na?"
"Can we stay till the power comes back? Even if it takes all night?"
"Till you fall asleep, Yogesh."

qa.q: What did Chacha say the white smudge was?
qa.a: Chacha said, "That's our galaxy. Millions of stars."

qa.q: What was Yogesh feeling while looking at the sky?
qa.a: Yogesh felt tiny but happy, full of wonder at so many stars, and puzzled that both feelings could exist together.

qa.q: Why did the lost match stop feeling big?
qa.a: Seeing how vast the sky was made Yogesh's own worry seem smaller, so the anger softened.

qa.q: How might Chacha have felt lying on the roof with Yogesh?
qa.a: Chacha likely felt calm and warm, enjoying Yogesh's wonder and happy to stay until Yogesh fell asleep.

grounding: A child under a night sky feels small yet strangely happy, and awe softens anger about a lost match.

passage:
Tuesday
Today was supposed to be terrible. Maths test, and I'd fought with Mummy about the phone, and I was angry all the way to the bus stop.
Then something happened. There was a little boy at the stop, shivering, no sweater, crying because he'd missed his school bus. An old lady, Kalyani Aunty from the flower stall, came out, took off her own shawl, wrapped him in it, and gave him a glass of hot tea from her flask. She didn't even know him. She waited with him until his father came.
I just stood there. Something in my chest went huge and quiet. Like when I heard the gurdwara kirtan at dawn last Gurpurab. My maths test, the fight, everything, suddenly looked so small.
In the test I was calm. I think I did okay.
Tonight I said sorry to Mummy.
Jasleen

qa.q: What did Kalyani Aunty give the boy from her flask?
qa.a: She gave him a glass of hot tea from her flask.

qa.q: What was Jasleen feeling while watching Kalyani Aunty?
qa.a: Jasleen felt awe and deep quiet, moved by the stranger's kindness, as the anger and worry shrank.

qa.q: What could Jasleen carry forward from this morning?
qa.a: Remembering moments of kindness or beauty, like Kalyani Aunty's shawl, can lift daily worries and help Jasleen stay calm.

qa.q: How might the little boy have felt when Kalyani Aunty wrapped him up?
qa.a: The boy likely felt comforted and safe after feeling cold, scared and alone.

grounding: A teenager is moved by a stranger's kindness and feels lifted beyond daily worries, showing awe can come from moral beauty.

passage:
Saturday night, Sandakphu trekkers' hut
Ganga had to drag me here. For months I said I had no time: deadlines, the flat lease, my manager's endless emails. I was snapping at everyone.
We walked for three days. My legs hated me. And this morning at 4:30 we climbed the ridge in the dark, shivering, and waited.
Then the sun hit Kanchenjunga. The whole range went pink, then gold. Four of the world's highest peaks in one line. Nobody spoke. Ganga held my arm.
I cried a little, honestly. Not sad. Just... overwhelmed by how big it was, and how small my inbox was next to it.
Tonight I haven't thought about the lease once. I'm going to put a trip like this in the calendar every year, before I need it.
Anirban

qa.q: What time did Anirban and Ganga climb the ridge?
qa.a: They climbed the ridge in the dark at 4:30.

qa.q: What was Anirban feeling when the sun hit Kanchenjunga?
qa.a: Anirban felt overwhelmed with awe, crying a little, not from sadness but from how vast the mountains were.

qa.q: What does Anirban plan to do, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Anirban plans a trip like this every year before needing it, because deliberate awe eases petty stress.

qa.q: How might Ganga have felt as they watched the sunrise together?
qa.a: Ganga likely felt happy and moved, glad to have dragged Anirban along, holding Anirban's arm in the quiet.

grounding: A young adult makes time for a trek and sunrise, and deliberate awe shrinks petty stress into perspective.

passage:
So, the thing I remember most from the Rann of Kutch trip isn't the photos. My name's Afreen, and I went with my friend Nirmala last December.
We'd driven out to the white salt desert for the full moon. Everyone else was taking selfies and chatting. Nirmala walked a little way off, and I followed. The moon came up over that endless white, and the whole ground started glowing.
Nirmala just stopped. She went completely quiet. I could see her breathing change, slower, and her hand came up to her mouth.
My instinct was to say something, "Wow, isn't it amazing?" I actually opened my mouth.
But I closed it. It felt like her moment. I stood next to her and just looked.
We stood there for maybe twenty minutes without a word.
On the drive back she said, "Thank you for not talking. I didn't want to come back yet."

qa.q: When did Afreen and Nirmala go to the Rann of Kutch?
qa.a: They went last December, for the full moon.

qa.q: Why did Afreen stay silent beside Nirmala?
qa.a: Afreen sensed that Nirmala was deeply moved and felt a gentle, protective respect for Nirmala's moment of awe.

qa.q: Why was Afreen's silence a kindness?
qa.a: By not filling the quiet with talk, Afreen let Nirmala stay fully inside the moment instead of being pulled back.

qa.q: How did Nirmala experience the silence?
qa.a: Nirmala felt grateful and at peace, thanking Afreen because she didn't want to come back to ordinary talk yet.

grounding: Someone standing with a friend before a great view sees the friend go quiet and lets the awe breathe without talking.

Monday. Lavanya woke from a bad dream, crying. Vaibhav picked her up and sat in the big chair, holding her against his chest. He breathed slowly, in and out, and didn't talk. Soon Lavanya's breaths slowed to match his. She fell asleep.
Thursday. Lavanya fell off her scooter and scraped her knee. After the plaster, she climbed into Papa's lap. "Breathe with me, Papa." They breathed. Her sobs faded.
Next Sunday. Vaibhav saw Lavanya on her bed, holding her crying doll. "Shh," she said, rocking. "Breathe slow, like Papa." She breathed in and out, very seriously.

qa.q: What did Lavanya say to her doll on Sunday?
qa.a: She said, "Shh. Breathe slow, like Papa."

qa.q: How did Lavanya feel after breathing with Papa on Thursday?
qa.a: Lavanya felt calmer and comforted, her sobs fading as she matched his slow breathing.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav do that helped Lavanya most?
qa.a: He stayed calm, held her and breathed slowly without talking, lending her his calm until she could share it.

qa.q: What might Vaibhav have felt seeing Lavanya with her doll?
qa.a: Vaibhav likely felt touched and proud, seeing she had stored his calm as a memory of safety.

grounding: A child borrows calm from a parent's slow breathing and stores it as a felt memory of safety.

passage:
I'm Arohi, and I used to explode when my little brother wrecked my things. I'd scream, throw stuff, cry for an hour.
One quiet Sunday, when I wasn't angry at all, my big cousin Raghav taught me three things. "When you feel it coming, breathe out slowly like blowing a candle, five times. Drink a glass of water. Step outside for a minute." We practised them on the balcony like a game.
Two weeks later my brother tore my comic. I felt the heat rising. And I remembered the candle. I blew out five slow breaths, drank water, went out on the balcony.
I was still angry. But not exploding angry. When I came back, I told him, "That was my favourite comic," and he said sorry.
I think it worked because I learned it on a calm day.

qa.q: How many slow breaths did Raghav tell Arohi to take?
qa.a: Raghav said to breathe out slowly like blowing a candle, five times.

qa.q: What was Arohi feeling when the comic was torn?
qa.a: Arohi felt anger heating up, but after the breaths it softened to plain anger instead of an explosion.

qa.q: Why did Raghav's calming steps work?
qa.a: They were taught and practised on a calm day like a game, so Arohi could remember them when upset.

qa.q: What would change if Raghav had taught the steps during one of Arohi's explosions?
qa.a: Arohi would likely have been too upset to listen, and the steps might have felt like being told off.

grounding: A child learns calming steps on a calm day and uses them when upset, since skills taught before the storm work better.

passage:
People ask how I got through my final-year viva, so here's the honest version. I'm Anand, and I was terrified.
The night before, I couldn't eat. My hands shook when I ironed my shirt. Professor Shankar, the external examiner, had a reputation: he'd once made a student redo a whole chapter.
But over the months I'd practised something my hostel warden taught me. I'd write two lists: what I can control, what I can't. Can control: knowing my data, sleeping, arriving early. Can't: his mood, his questions, whether he likes my topic.
In the morning I read the lists again. The fear was still there, a knot in my stomach. But I stopped fighting it.
When Professor Shankar asked a question I didn't know, I said, "I haven't tested that. My guess is this, and here's how I'd check." He nodded.
I passed. Not because I wasn't scared. Because I let the fear sit there and did my part anyway.

qa.q: Who was the external examiner?
qa.a: Professor Shankar was the external examiner.

qa.q: What was Anand feeling the night before the viva?
qa.a: Anand felt terrified and anxious, unable to eat, with shaking hands.

qa.q: What practice helped Anand stay steady, and why?
qa.a: Writing lists of what could and couldn't be controlled helped Anand accept the uncontrollable parts and focus on preparation.

qa.q: How might Professor Shankar have seen Anand's honest answer?
qa.a: Professor Shankar likely respected it, since Anand admitted what was untested and showed how to check it, which earned a nod.

grounding: A student feels nerves before a viva yet stays steady by accepting what cannot be controlled, showing calm as a practised stance.

"Hafsa, you're panicking about tomorrow's launch. Sit. Let your Chetan Chacha tell you about the day I learnt what calm is.
"I was twenty-four, my first big client presentation in Delhi. Fifteen minutes before, my laptop died. Completely. I started sweating, pacing, dialling everyone. My heart was going like a drum.
"My senior, Mrs Rao, was sitting in the corner with her tea. She looked up and said, very slowly, 'Chetan. Sit down. We have paper. We have your brain. Tell me the three main points.'
"Something about her voice. My breathing slowed just listening to her. I sat. I told her the three points. She wrote them on a flip chart in big letters.
"We presented with a marker and a flip chart. The client said it was the clearest pitch they'd seen.
"I never forgot how her calm spilled into me. Be that for someone one day, Hafsa.

qa.q: What did Mrs Rao ask young Chetan to tell her?
qa.a: She asked him to tell her the three main points.

qa.q: What was young Chetan feeling when the laptop died?
qa.a: Young Chetan felt panicked, sweating and pacing, with his heart going like a drum.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Chetan Chacha's story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Mrs Rao's slow, steady voice telling him to sit down; her calm eased his panic enough to think clearly and present with a flip chart.

qa.q: How did Mrs Rao likely feel during those fifteen minutes?
qa.a: Mrs Rao likely felt steady and confident, trusting that the ideas mattered more than the laptop.

grounding: An elder recalls his panic easing near a calm senior, showing that calm spreads and being steady for others is a gift.

"Himani, what do you say to Dadi for the new frock?"
"...Thank you."
"Nicely, beta."
"Thank you, Dadi," Himani mumbled, already running to try it on.
Later, at dinner, Chetan passed his mother the dal. "Thank you, Amma. It's perfect today."
Himani watched. "Papa, why do you say thank you to Dadi? She's your mummy."
"Because she cooked for us. It makes her happy."
Himani thought about it. When Dadi passed her the papad, she said, "Thank you, Dadi," all by herself, and looked at Papa.
Papa smiled. Dadi smiled more.
